items: Understand the Impulse Control Gap: Recognize that your toddler lacks the brain hardware to stop themselves on command—this is developmental, not defiant.
Reframe Hitting as a Timing Problem: Remember that your toddler's prefrontal cortex won't be fully online for another twenty years, so they're not choosing to be difficult.
Become Your Child's External Regulation System: Act as the calm, external brain your child hasn't built yet by consistently scaffolding their responses until their own system develops.
Trust That Consistent Responses Build Neural Pathways: Each time you respond calmly to aggression, you're laying down brain wiring that will eventually support your child's own internal regulation.
Identify Your Child's Dominant Trigger: Pay attention to whether overstimulation, frustration, physical discomfort, or attention-seeking is driving most of your child's aggressive episodes.
Watch for Physical Warning Signs Before Aggression: Look for early body language cues like hand flapping, freezing, or sudden mood changes that signal dysregulation is building.
Notice Patterns in Timing and Environment: Track which times of day, settings, or situations tend to trigger your child's aggressive responses so you can prepare in advance.
Shift Your Focus to What Came Before: Instead of reacting to the hit, ask what warning signs appeared in the minutes leading up to it so you can intervene earlier.
Pause Before You React: When aggression happens, take a breath and ask what you're expecting your child to do that their brain physically cannot manage yet.
Scaffold with Words Instead of Punishment: Give your child the language for their overwhelming feelings by saying what you see, like 'You're so frustrated the tower fell down.'
Redirect Before the Amygdala Takes Over: When you spot the warning signs, step in early and redirect your child to a calming strategy before their alarm system drives the reaction.
Stay Calm and Predictable in Your Response: Provide the same calm, consistent scaffolding every time aggression happens so your child learns what a regulated response looks like.
